content: A fluid is a substance that continuously deforms, or flows, when subjected to any amount of shear stress, no matter how small the stress may be. Both liquids and gases fall under the category of fluids. Fluids are a subset of the phases of matter and include not only liquids and gases but also plasmas and, to a certain extent, plastic solids. One distinguishing feature of liquids is that they can form a free surface, which is a surface not determined by the shape of the container, whereas gases do not exhibit this property. The distinction between solids and fluids is not always straightforward and is often determined by evaluating the viscosity of the material. For example, Silly Putty can behave as either a solid or a fluid depending on the time scale over which it is observed. Fluids exhibit specific characteristics, such as their inability to resist deformation or their ability to resist it only slightly, which is quantified as viscosity. Additionally, fluids have the capacity to flow, meaning they can adapt to the shape of their container. These properties arise from the fact that fluids cannot sustain shear stress when in static equilibrium. In contrast, solids can withstand both shear stresses and normal stresses, which include compressive and tensile forces. Real fluids, due to their viscosity, can also experience low levels of shear stress. In solids, shear stress is dependent on the amount of strain, whereas in fluids, shear stress depends on the rate of strain. Fluids can be categorized based on the relationship between shear stress and the rate of strain. Newtonian fluids are those in which shear stress is directly proportional to the rate of strain. Non-Newtonian fluids, on the other hand, exhibit a more complex relationship where shear stress depends on the rate of strain, its higher powers, or its derivatives. The behavior of fluids is mathematically described by the Navier-Stokes equations, which are a set of partial differential equations. These equations are grounded in the principles of: Conservation of mass (continuity), Conservation of linear momentum, Conservation of angular momentum, and Conservation of energy. The scientific study of fluids is known as fluid mechanics. This field is further divided into fluid dynamics, which focuses on fluids in motion, and fluid statics, which examines fluids at rest.
